Status (the drafting log’s opening line):

Status: LIONESS edges, network metrics, and pathway connectivity and crosstalk are, to first order and in practice, fixed quadratic functions of the sample’s own expression, so over repeated visits they describe, explain, and predict as the expression scores do; there is no correction (pilot-f) and no fix, only a diagnostic (compare with the expression terms); prediction with pathway metrics and real gene sets has not been piloted.

The seven paper-test answers are in the drafting log.

Abstract

Background. LIONESS builds a co-expression network for each sample, and network metrics of those networks, read by pathway, are used as personal markers that should track a patient over repeated visits. What these metrics measure has not been derived.

Results. A Pearson LIONESS edge is an exact function of the cohort correlation and the sample’s own standardized expression, and a pathway’s connectivity and crosstalk are, to first order, the squared pathway score and the product of two scores. In simulated children followed over visits, every network metric, among them degree, betweenness, transitivity, and the numbers of edges and nodes, was as stable as the same metric on the first-order network (largest difference 0.0024); connectivity and crosstalk had \(R^2\) of at least 0.99999 on their expression terms, and the residual’s stability was at most 0.044 once fourth-order terms were added. Pathway scores predicted same-visit activity, with power up to 0.80, while LIONESS metrics were declared predictive in no replicate at any effect and were equivalent to first-order metrics in every replicate. In 131 children with lupus followed over 897 visits (GSE65391), LIONESS metrics of BloodGen3 pathways were as stable as their first-order versions (largest difference 0.0058), and predicted SLEDAI no better (concordance 0.523 against 0.628 for module scores).

Conclusions. The stability of a LIONESS network over a person’s visits is the stability of the person’s expression. A network metric should be compared with the expression terms of its closed form before it is read as co-expression.

1 Introduction

Blood is sampled again and again in people with lupus, to follow a disease that flares and remits [1]. A gene network for each sample promises to show how a patient’s co-expression changes from one visit to the next, beyond how much each gene is expressed. LIONESS builds such a network for each sample of a cohort: it compares the co-expression network of all samples with the network of all samples but one, and assigns the scaled difference to the sample left out [2]. With Pearson correlation as the network, the default of its R implementation, every sample receives one weight for every pair of genes [3]. In the paper that introduced lionessR, single-sample networks of bone tumours were built in this way, edges whose weights differed between patients with short and long metastasis-free survival were selected, and limma tested them, beside a separate test of expression levels [3]. A difference in a sample’s edge is read there as a difference in how that sample adds to the co-expression of the two genes. Co-expression is summarized by gene sets in two established ways: cohort networks by module eigengenes and module connectivity [4], and blood transcriptomes by fixed module repertoires [5]. For a single-sample network, the natural summaries of a pathway are the mean edge among its genes, its connectivity, and the mean edge between its genes and those of a second pathway, their crosstalk.

Repeated blood samples differ in expression between people and within a person over time. Blood gene expression is partly specific to the individual [6], the interferon signature of lupus is stable within patients [7], and cell composition drives much of the co-expression seen in bulk data [8]. A Pearson LIONESS edge between genes \(i\) and \(j\) in sample \(q\) is, to first order in \(1/N\) for a cohort of \(N\) samples, a function of that sample’s own standardized expression \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\) and of the cohort correlation \(r_{ij}\): \[ e_{qij} \approx r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2}\left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right). \tag{1}\] The product term is the single-sample correlation of earlier work [9]. Averaged over the pairs of a pathway, the product term becomes the square of the pathway’s summed expression, so a sample’s connectivity follows its pathway score. In a network built from all samples, module networks are approximately factorizable, and a gene’s connectivity has a counterpart computed from the module eigengene [10]. That result concerns connectivity across the genes of one cohort network. What has not been derived is the closed form of one sample’s pathway connectivity and crosstalk, and what it implies for their stability over a person’s visits and for their value as predictors.

We derive the exact closed form of a Pearson LIONESS edge and, from it, what the usual network metrics of a single-sample network measure when read through pathways: connectivity, crosstalk, total edge weight, strength, degree, betweenness, transitivity, and the numbers of edges and nodes. We then ask three questions. How much do these LIONESS metrics change across a person’s visits? Is that change the change in the person’s own expression, as the closed forms say? Do the LIONESS metrics identify a person and predict disease activity, at the same visit and at the next, better than pathway expression scores, and differently from the same metrics computed on the first-order form of the edges? In the Methods, we give the closed forms and a diagnostic that compares a network metric with its expression terms. In a simulation study of repeated visits, we vary how stable and how strong a pathway’s driving factor is, the pathway’s size, and person-specific co-expression. Finally, we follow children with lupus over repeated visits and apply the same analyses to their blood.

2 Methods

We first define LIONESS networks and the metrics read from them through pathways (Section 2.1, Section 2.2), then derive what the edges and the metrics measure (Section 2.3), and give a diagnostic that follows from that result (Section 2.4). We then define how we measured the stability of a metric over a person’s visits (Section 2.5), whether it identifies the person (Section 2.6), and how well it predicts disease activity (Section 2.7), and close with the data and the software.

2.1 LIONESS single-sample networks

A user who builds a LIONESS network for a blood sample reads it as the co-expression specific to that sample, and reads a network metric of it, such as the connectivity of the interferon genes, as how tightly that pathway’s genes move together in that person at that visit. Over repeated visits, the stability of the metric is then read as the stability of the person’s network. The procedure is the following. Consider a cohort of \(N\) samples, indexed by \(q\), measured on \(p\) genes, indexed by \(i\) and \(j\). Let \(r_{ij}\) be the Pearson correlation of genes \(i\) and \(j\) over all \(N\) samples, and \(r^{(-q)}_{ij}\) their correlation over the \(N - 1\) samples left when sample \(q\) is removed. The LIONESS edge between genes \(i\) and \(j\) in sample \(q\) is [2] \[ e_{qij} = N r_{ij} - (N - 1)\, r^{(-q)}_{ij}. \tag{2}\] The edge is large and positive when leaving sample \(q\) out lowers the correlation of the two genes, and large and negative when leaving it out raises it; the factor \(N - 1\) scales one sample’s influence up to the size of a correlation. Every metric in this paper is built from the edges of Equation 2, so what an edge measures decides what every metric measures. For that reason the rest of this section starts from the edge.

2.2 Network metrics read through pathways

A pathway is a set of genes; let \(A\) be a pathway of \(m_A\) genes and \(B\) a second pathway of \(m_B\) genes, with no gene in common with \(A\). For sample \(q\), the connectivity \(W_{qA}\) of pathway \(A\) is the mean edge among its genes, \[ W_{qA} = \binom{m_A}{2}^{-1} \sum_{i < j \in A} e_{qij}, \tag{3}\] where \(\binom{m_A}{2} = m_A (m_A - 1)/2\) is the number of pairs of genes in \(A\) and the sum runs over those pairs. The crosstalk \(X_{qAB}\) between pathways \(A\) and \(B\) is the mean edge between their genes, \[ X_{qAB} = \frac{1}{m_A m_B} \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} e_{qij}, \tag{4}\] where the sums pair every gene \(i\) of \(A\) with every gene \(j\) of \(B\). The total edge weight \(T_q\) is the sum of all edges of the network, and the strength \(s_{qi}\) of gene \(i\) the sum of its edges, \[ T_q = \sum_{i < j} e_{qij}, \qquad s_{qi} = \sum_{j \ne i} e_{qij}, \tag{5}\] where the first sum runs over all pairs of the \(p\) genes and the second over the \(p - 1\) genes other than \(i\). For the graph metrics, we kept in a graph \(G_q\) the pairs with \(\lvert e_{qij}\rvert\) above a threshold, either fixed or chosen so that a fixed share of pairs is kept, and computed the number of edges and of nodes (genes with at least one edge) of \(G_q\), its transitivity (the share of connected triples that close into triangles), and each gene’s degree and betweenness, the latter with distance \(1/\lvert e_{qij}\rvert\). We averaged the gene-level metrics over the genes of each pathway. Reading the network through pathways turns many thousands of edges per sample into a few numbers with a biological label. The metrics fall into two groups: sums of edges (Equation 3, Equation 4, and Equation 5) and functions of the edges above a threshold (degree, betweenness, transitivity, and the numbers of edges and nodes). A closed form for the edge therefore carries over exactly to the first group and constrains the second.

2.3 What LIONESS edges and metrics measure

We show that every LIONESS edge is an exact function of the cohort correlation and the sample’s own standardized expression. Let \(x_{qi}\) be the expression of gene \(i\) in sample \(q\), and let \[ z_{qi} = \frac{x_{qi} - \bar x_i}{\sigma_i}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{1}{N - 1}, \tag{6}\] where \(\bar x_i\) is the mean of gene \(i\) over all \(N\) samples, \(\sigma_i\) its standard deviation with divisor \(N\), so that \(z_{qi}\) is the number of standard deviations by which sample \(q\) lies above the cohort mean of gene \(i\), and \(\varepsilon\) is a small number that shrinks as the cohort grows. Removing sample \(q\) changes the correlation to (supplement, S1.1) \[ r^{(-q)}_{ij} = \frac{r_{ij} - \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj}}{\sqrt{(1 - \varepsilon z_{qi}^2)(1 - \varepsilon z_{qj}^2)}}, \tag{7}\] so that, by Equation 2, the edge is \[ e_{qij} = N r_{ij} - (N - 1)\, \frac{r_{ij} - \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj}}{\sqrt{(1 - \varepsilon z_{qi}^2)(1 - \varepsilon z_{qj}^2)}}. \tag{8}\] In Equation 8, \(r_{ij}\) is the cohort correlation of the two genes and \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\) are the sample’s two standardized values; nothing else enters. This is the central result of the paper. For a given cohort, the edge of sample \(q\) is fixed once the sample’s two standardized values are known: the rest of the cohort enters only through the correlation \(r_{ij}\) and the standardization of Equation 6. Two samples with the same \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\) therefore receive the same edge, whatever the rest of their expression, and an edge carries no information about the sample beyond these two numbers. Expanding Equation 8 in powers of \(\varepsilon\) gives the first-order form and a remainder (S1.2): \[ e_{qij} = r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2}\left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right) + O(\varepsilon), \tag{9}\] where \(O(\varepsilon)\) stands for a term no larger than a constant times \(\varepsilon\), which vanishes as the cohort grows and is a polynomial of degree four in \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\). This is the form given in Equation 1 of the Introduction. Each of its three terms has a plain reading. The first, \(r_{ij}\), is the same for every sample. The second, \(z_{qi} z_{qj}\), is positive when the sample lies on the same side of the cohort mean for both genes and negative when it lies on opposite sides, and it grows with how far the sample lies from the mean. The third pulls the edge back toward the cohort correlation when either value is large. A sample far from the mean on both genes therefore receives a strong edge between them, whether or not the two genes are co-regulated in that person.

Summing Equation 9 over the pairs of a pathway gives the connectivity and crosstalk as linear functions of three expression terms each (S1.3). For pathway \(A\) and sample \(q\), let \[ S_A = \sum_{i \in A} z_{qi}, \qquad Q_A = \sum_{i \in A} z_{qi}^2, \qquad R^B_i = \sum_{j \in B,\, j \ne i} r_{ij}, \tag{10}\] where \(S_A\) is the sum of the sample’s standardized values over the genes of \(A\), \(Q_A\) the sum of their squares, and \(R^B_i\) the summed cohort correlation of gene \(i\) with the genes of \(B\) (\(R^A_i\) is the same with the other genes of \(A\)). With \(C_A = \binom{m_A}{2}\) the number of pairs in \(A\), \(\bar r_A\) the mean cohort correlation among the genes of \(A\), and \(\bar r_{AB}\) the mean cohort correlation between the genes of \(A\) and of \(B\), the connectivity of Equation 3 and the crosstalk of Equation 4 are, to first order, \[ W_{qA} \approx \bar r_A + \frac{S_A^2 - Q_A}{2 C_A} - \frac{1}{2 C_A} \sum_{i \in A} R^A_i z_{qi}^2, \tag{11}\] \[ X_{qAB} \approx \bar r_{AB} + \frac{S_A S_B}{m_A m_B} - \frac{1}{2 m_A m_B} \Big( \sum_{i \in A} R^B_i z_{qi}^2 + \sum_{j \in B} R^A_j z_{qj}^2 \Big). \tag{12}\] The pathway score of \(A\) in sample \(q\) is the mean standardized expression of its genes, \(S_A/m_A\). By Equation 11, the connectivity is, up to small terms, the squared pathway score \((S_A/m_A)^2\); by Equation 12, the crosstalk is, up to small terms, the product of two pathway scores. Two consequences follow. First, a pathway’s connectivity is high when its genes lie, on average, far from the cohort mean in either direction: it records how unusual the pathway’s level is in that sample, not its direction, so a sample with the pathway strongly up and one with it strongly down both receive a high connectivity. Second, to first order, connectivity and crosstalk hold no information beyond the standardized expression of the pathways’ own genes and the cohort correlations. The total edge weight of Equation 5 is the same sum over all genes, and the strength of gene \(i\) is, to first order (S1.4), \[ s_{qi} \approx R_i + z_{qi}(S - z_{qi}) - \tfrac{1}{2} R_i z_{qi}^2 - \tfrac12 \sum_{j \ne i} r_{ij} z_{qj}^2, \tag{13}\] where \(S = \sum_{j} z_{qj}\) is the sum of the sample’s standardized values over all \(p\) genes and \(R_i = \sum_{j \ne i} r_{ij}\) the summed cohort correlation of gene \(i\) with all other genes. The graph metrics have no closed form, but they are functions of the edges of Equation 8, and so of the same standardized expression. A metric is therefore stable over a person’s visits to the extent that the person’s expression terms are: the squared score of a pathway driven by a factor whose within-person intraclass correlation (Equation 14) is \(\kappa\) has intraclass correlation \(\kappa^2\) when the factor is normal (S1.5). This makes the stability of a metric predictable: a metric that squares an expression term is as stable as that square, and less stable than the term itself, since \(\kappa^2 < \kappa\) whenever \(0 < \kappa < 1\).

2.4 A diagnostic: comparing a metric with its expression terms

We propose two checks that tell a user whether a LIONESS metric carries anything beyond the sample’s expression. In the first, we recompute the metric on the first-order form of the edges (Equation 9 without the remainder), the network that the closed form predicts from expression alone, and compare the two metrics’ stability over visits and their predictions. In the second, we regress connectivity and crosstalk over samples on their three first-order expression terms of Equation 11 and Equation 12, then with the fourth-order terms of the remainder added (\(S_A^4\), \(S_A^2 Q_A\), \(Q_A^2\), and \(\sum_{i \in A} z_{qi}^4\) for connectivity; the corresponding products for crosstalk), and report the \(R^2\) and the stability of the residual. A metric that matches its first-order version, and whose residual is not stable, measures expression. The two checks answer different questions. The first applies to every metric, including the graph metrics that have no closed form, and asks whether the LIONESS network gives a metric anything that the expression-only network does not. The second applies to connectivity and crosstalk, whose closed forms name the terms, and asks how much of the metric those terms explain and whether what remains is stable over visits. A metric that fails either check carries something beyond expression; for a metric that passes both, its expression terms serve in its place without loss.

2.5 Stability over visits

For each feature set, a vector of numbers for person \(p\) at visit \(v\) (the LIONESS metrics, the first-order metrics, the pathway scores, or the genes), we measured how stable it is over a person’s visits, whether it identifies the person, and how well it predicts disease activity at the same visit and at the next one. For one feature, let \(u_{pv}\) be its value for person \(p\) at visit \(v\), \(n_p\) the number of visits of person \(p\), \(P\) the number of people, and \(n = \sum_p n_p\) the number of samples; let \(\bar u_{p\cdot}\) be the mean of person \(p\)’s visits and \(\bar u_{\cdot\cdot}\) the mean of all samples. We used the one-way intraclass correlation \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{MSB} &= \frac{1}{P - 1} \sum_{p} n_p \left(\bar u_{p\cdot} - \bar u_{\cdot\cdot}\right)^2, \\ \mathrm{MSW} &= \frac{1}{n - P} \sum_{p} \sum_{v} \left(u_{pv} - \bar u_{p\cdot}\right)^2, \\ n_0 &= \frac{1}{P - 1}\Big(n - \frac{1}{n}\sum_p n_p^2\Big), \\ I &= \frac{\mathrm{MSB} - \mathrm{MSW}}{\mathrm{MSB} + (n_0 - 1)\,\mathrm{MSW}}, \end{aligned} \tag{14}\] where MSB is the mean square between people (how far the people’s means lie from the overall mean), MSW the mean square within people (how far a person’s visits lie from that person’s mean), and \(n_0\) the average number of visits per person, corrected for unequal numbers. \(I\) is the share of the feature’s variance that belongs to the person rather than to the visit: it is zero when a person’s visits differ as much as different people do, and one when every visit of a person gives the same value. We chose this measure because the question a user asks of a personal network is whether it stays with the person, and the intraclass correlation of Equation 14 answers it directly: it weighs the differences within a person over time against the differences between people. It also allows people to have different numbers of visits, as in the application. And because a metric that squares an expression term has the square of that term’s stability (S1.5), the intraclass correlation also tests the closed forms against data.

2.6 Identification of a person

For each person, let \(\mathbf{f}_{p1}\) and \(\mathbf{f}_{p2}\) be the feature vectors of the first two visits, each feature standardized over all samples. The person predicted for the second visit of person \(p\) is the person whose first visit is most correlated with it, and the fingerprinting accuracy is the share of people predicted correctly [11]: \[ \hat p = \arg\max_{p'} \operatorname{cor}\left(\mathbf{f}_{p2}, \mathbf{f}_{p'1}\right), \qquad \mathrm{Acc} = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{p} \mathbb{1}\left(\hat p = p\right), \tag{15}\] where \(p'\) runs over all \(P\) people, \(\operatorname{cor}\) is the Pearson correlation over the features, \(\hat p\) is the person whose first visit correlates most with the second visit of person \(p\), and \(\mathbb{1}(\cdot)\) is one when its condition holds and zero otherwise; guessing gives \(\mathrm{Acc} = 1/P\). Identification is a stronger test of a personal network than stability: a network specific to a person should single that person out among all others from one visit to the next. Comparing the accuracy of Equation 15 for the LIONESS metrics with that for the first-order metrics and for the genes asks whether any identifying information lies in the network rather than in the expression it is built from.

2.7 Prediction of disease activity

Throughout, \(\mathbf{s}_{pv}\) is the vector of pathway scores of person \(p\) at visit \(v\) (the mean standardized expression of each pathway’s genes), \(\mathbf{s}^{2}_{pv}\) its elementwise square, \(\mathbf{g}_{pv}\) the standardized expression of all genes of the network, \(\mathbf{m}_{pv}\) the LIONESS metrics of Section 2.2, \(\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{pv}\) the same metrics computed on the first-order network, and \(y_{pv}\) the disease activity (SLEDAI in the application). The models named A, B, and C below are not the pathways \(A\) and \(B\) of Section 2.2.

2.7.1 The common form of the models

Every model predicts activity at the same visit as \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{b}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}^\top \mathbf{w}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}, \tag{16}\] and at the next visit as \[ y_{p,v+1} = \alpha + \delta\, y_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{b}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}^\top \mathbf{w}_{pv} + \xi_{p,v+1}, \tag{17}\] where \(\alpha\) is an intercept, \(\mathbf{b}_{pv}\) the model’s base terms with coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\), \(\mathbf{w}_{pv}\) its features under test with coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), \(\delta\) the coefficient of the current activity, and \(\xi\) an error with mean zero. The base terms and the current activity are not penalized; the features under test are, by the elastic net [12], which over the \(n_{\mathrm{tr}}\) training samples minimizes \[ \frac{1}{2n_{\mathrm{tr}}} \sum_{t = 1}^{n_{\mathrm{tr}}} \left(y_t - \alpha - \delta y^{\mathrm{cur}}_t - \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\top \mathbf{b}_t - \boldsymbol{\theta}^\top \mathbf{w}_t\right)^2 + \lambda \left[\frac{1 - a}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{\theta} \rVert_2^2 + a \lVert \boldsymbol{\theta} \rVert_1\right], \tag{18}\] where \(t\) indexes the training samples, \(y_t\) is the activity to be predicted, \(y^{\mathrm{cur}}_t\) the current activity (absent, \(\delta = 0\), for same-visit prediction), \(\lVert \boldsymbol{\theta} \rVert_2^2\) the sum of the squared coefficients and \(\lVert \boldsymbol{\theta} \rVert_1\) the sum of their absolute values, \(a\) the mixing between the two penalties, set to 0.50, and \(\lambda\) the strength of the penalty, chosen by 5-fold cross-validation inside the training samples, with all visits of a person in one fold, at the value with the smallest mean squared error. A model with no features under test was fitted by least squares, that is, Equation 18 with \(\lambda = 0\). Every prediction was made out of fold: the people were split into 5 folds, and each person’s predictions came from a model fitted on the other folds. The models below differ only in \(\mathbf{b}_{pv}\) and \(\mathbf{w}_{pv}\); moving up the ladder from R0 to N1 adds one source of information at a time. Two choices keep the comparison fair. The base terms are left unpenalized, so that each model starts from the same information and the penalty acts only on what the model adds. And the folds keep all visits of a person together, because a person’s visits resemble one another, and a model trained on one of them predicts the others too well.

2.7.2 Model R0: the current activity alone

R0 predicts the next visit from today’s activity only, and is the floor any expression model must beat for the next visit: \[ y_{p,v+1} = \alpha + \delta\, y_{pv} + \xi_{p,v+1}, \tag{19}\] fitted by least squares. It is Equation 17 with no base terms and no features under test, and has no same-visit version, since it has no predictor at the same visit. Activity is partly stable within a person, so R0 is the bar every other model must clear for the next visit: a model whose next-visit concordance (Equation 27) does not exceed that of R0 has learned nothing from expression.

2.7.3 Model R1: the pathway scores

R1 uses the pathway scores and their squares, the expression terms that the closed forms (Equation 11, Equation 12) say the LIONESS metrics are made of: \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_1^\top \mathbf{s}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_2^\top \mathbf{s}^{2}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}, \tag{20}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_2\) hold one unpenalized coefficient per pathway for the score and its square; the model is fitted by least squares, and for the next visit \(\delta\, y_{pv}\) is added. R1 is the simplest model that holds what the closed forms say the LIONESS metrics contain; if the metrics carry nothing more, the models built on them do no better than R1.

2.7.4 Model E1: the genes

E1 adds every gene of the network, penalized, to the terms of R1: \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_1^\top \mathbf{s}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_2^\top \mathbf{s}^{2}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}_g^\top \mathbf{g}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}, \tag{21}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_g\) holds one penalized coefficient per gene; for the next visit, \(\delta\, y_{pv}\) is added. E1 is the expression baseline: everything the network is built from. Comparing E1 with R1 shows how much the individual genes add to their pathway averages.

2.7.5 Model N1: the genes and the LIONESS metrics

N1 adds the LIONESS metrics, penalized, to E1: \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_1^\top \mathbf{s}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_2^\top \mathbf{s}^{2}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}_g^\top \mathbf{g}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}_m^\top \mathbf{m}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}, \tag{22}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_m\) holds one penalized coefficient per metric; for the next visit, \(\delta\, y_{pv}\) is added. The contrast \(\Delta_1 = C(\mathrm{N1}) - C(\mathrm{E1})\), with \(C\) the concordance of Equation 27, is what the LIONESS network adds to the genes. If the LIONESS network carries co-expression that the genes do not, N1 exceeds E1. The closed forms imply that it does not, since by Equation 8 every metric is a function of the genes’ standardized values and the cohort correlations; \(\Delta_1\) tests that implication.

2.7.6 Model F1: the genes and the first-order metrics

F1 is N1 with the LIONESS metrics replaced by the same metrics computed on the first-order network: \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_1^\top \mathbf{s}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\gamma}_2^\top \mathbf{s}^{2}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}_g^\top \mathbf{g}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}_f^\top \mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}, \tag{23}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_f\) holds one penalized coefficient per first-order metric; for the next visit, \(\delta\, y_{pv}\) is added. The contrast \(\Delta_2 = C(\mathrm{N1}) - C(\mathrm{F1})\) is what the LIONESS network adds to its own first-order form. Equivalence of N1 and F1 means that whatever the LIONESS metrics contribute to prediction is already in their first-order form, which is a function of expression alone.

2.7.7 Model A: the LIONESS metrics alone

A uses only the LIONESS metrics, penalized, with no base terms: \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\theta}_m^\top \mathbf{m}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}. \tag{24}\] A is the prediction available to a user who reads only the network.

2.7.8 Model B: the pathway scores, penalized

B uses the pathway scores and their squares like R1 (Equation 20), but penalized, so that it is fitted the same way as A and C: \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\theta}_1^\top \mathbf{s}_{pv} + \boldsymbol{\theta}_2^\top \mathbf{s}^{2}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}, \tag{25}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_2\) are the penalized counterparts of \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_1\) and \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_2\). B keeps the sign of each pathway score, which the metrics lose when they square it (Equation 11); comparing A with B shows what that loss costs.

2.7.9 Model C: the first-order metrics alone

C is A (Equation 24) with the first-order metrics in place of the LIONESS metrics: \[ y_{pv} = \alpha + \boldsymbol{\theta}_f^\top \mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{pv} + \xi_{pv}. \tag{26}\] For the next visit, A, B, and C each add \(\delta\, y_{pv}\) unpenalized. Comparing A with C repeats the contrast of N1 with F1 without the genes.

2.7.10 Scoring and tests

Predictions were scored by the concordance \[ C = \frac{\sum_{(k, l):\, y_k > y_l} \left[\mathbb{1}(\hat y_k > \hat y_l) + \tfrac12\, \mathbb{1}(\hat y_k = \hat y_l)\right]}{\#\{(k, l): y_k > y_l\}}, \tag{27}\] where \(k\) and \(l\) index samples, \(y_k\) is the observed activity of sample \(k\), \(\hat y_k\) its out-of-fold prediction, the sums run over the pairs of samples whose activity differs, and \(\#\{\cdot\}\) counts those pairs. \(C\) is the share of such pairs that the predictions put in the right order, ties counting one half; \(C = 1/2\) is chance and \(C = 1\) a perfect ordering (S1.6). To test, we drew \(B^{*} = 200\) bootstrap samples of people, with replacement and with all of a person’s visits, and recomputed Equation 27 as \(C^{*}_b\) for each bootstrap sample \(b = 1, \dots, B^{*}\) without refitting. With \(Q_{\pi}(\cdot)\) the \(\pi\) quantile over the bootstrap samples, the decisions were \[ \begin{aligned} \text{better than chance:}\quad & Q_{0.05}(C^{*}) > \tfrac12, \\ M_1 \text{ better than } M_2:\quad & Q_{0.05}(\Delta^{*}) > 0, \\ M_1 \text{ equivalent to } M_2:\quad & \left[Q_{0.05}(\Delta^{*}),\, Q_{0.95}(\Delta^{*})\right] \subset (-\eta, \eta), \end{aligned} \tag{28}\] where \(\Delta^{*}\) is the bootstrap difference \(C^{*}(M_1) - C^{*}(M_2)\) between two models \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) and \(\eta = 0.05\) is the equivalence margin. We scored by concordance because it depends only on the order of the predictions, so that models fitted on different terms are compared on the same scale. We resampled people rather than visits because the visits of one person are not independent. And we tested equivalence as well as superiority because failing to show that one model is better is not evidence that two models are the same; the equivalence test makes that claim directly, within a stated margin.

2.8 Data

For the application, we used the longitudinal study of children with systemic lupus erythematosus of [1], Gene Expression Omnibus series GSE65391, whole-blood expression on the Illumina HumanHT-12 array with disease activity (SLEDAI) recorded at every visit. We kept the 131 children with two or more visits, 897 visits in all, ordered by time within child, and the authors’ split into training and test children. We mapped probes to gene symbols with the platform table, keeping for each gene the probe with the highest mean expression, and dropped genes with no variance or with variance in a single sample only (for which the leave-one-out correlation is undefined), leaving 10,084 genes that belong to a module. We took the modules of the BloodGen3 repertoire, built from co-clustering in blood transcriptomes of sixteen immunological and physiological states [5], from its R package [13], and analysed one by one the 382 modules with at least 10 genes on the array. We built the network over the genes of four pathways, which we chose by their BloodGen3 function label before computing any network: interferon (103 genes), neutrophil (145), lymphocyte (181), and plasma cell (106). We computed each child’s LIONESS network and its first-order version sample by sample from the exact closed form, and used the metrics, feature sets, and tests of the simulation study, with SLEDAI as the activity.

2.9 Software and reproducibility

We organized the code as a research compendium [14]: an R package whose functions are documented and tested, analysis scripts that call those functions and write every result to a results folder, and this manuscript, which reads only from that folder, so that every number, table, and figure in it is computed from the saved results when the document is rendered. Each simulation cell has its own random seed, derived from the design table, and we saved the per-replicate results rather than summaries. We recorded the software and package versions with the results.

We used R version 4.6.2 (2026-10-29), with glmnet [12] for the elastic net and igraph for the graph metrics.

2.10 Use of AI

We used an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) to draft the analysis code, to propose the structure of the simulation study, to summarize the literature, and to produce a first draft of the text; we directed and reviewed the work throughout. We reviewed, corrected, and take responsibility for every part of the manuscript and the code. We checked every derivation numerically, and we verify every citation against the cited paper before submission. The figures are drawn from simulated data and computed results by code in the accompanying repository. No AI tool is an author.

TO CONFIRM: whether the journal wants the figure legends to name the AI-assisted code

3 Simulation study

3.1 Design

The simulation study is reported in the ADEMP structure [15]: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, and performance measures, with a Monte Carlo standard error for every reported rate and average.

The study has three aims, the paper’s questions: how stable over a person’s visits each LIONESS metric is (aim 1); whether that stability equals the stability of the same metric on the first-order network, and whether connectivity and crosstalk are their expression terms (aim 2); and whether LIONESS metrics identify a person and predict activity better than pathway scores, or differently from first-order metrics (aim 3).

Every simulated cohort had 131 people, the number of children with two or more visits in the application, and ninety or more genes in six pathways. Four pathways each loaded on their own factor, a person level plus a visit deviation: an interferon-like pathway, whose factor’s within-person intraclass correlation, loading, and size were varied, and neutrophil-like, lymphocyte-like, and plasmablast-like pathways with loading 0.60 and intraclass correlations 0.41, 0.48, and 0.39, the values measured in the application for the neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages and for disease activity. A fifth pathway had a noise correlation that differed between people by up to the spread \(\tau\) (person-specific co-expression), and a sixth had a fixed noise correlation. Every gene carried a person level of variance 0.50 and unit normal noise, and the factors were independent. Each visit had an activity score: the activity effect \(\beta\) times the mean of the interferon and plasmablast factors, plus a person level and visit noise with within-person intraclass correlation 0.39. Study S1 varied one factor at a time around a base setting at the measured values (Table 1), and added a null setting with no stable factor and no person-specific co-expression, where every residual stability is zero. Study S2 used the base setting with 5 activity effects, the first zero, which gives the tests’ type I error and power.

The estimands were the intraclass correlation over visits of every metric, on the LIONESS network and on its first-order form, and their difference; for connectivity and crosstalk, the \(R^2\) on the expression terms of first and of fourth order and the stability of each residual; fingerprinting accuracy, the share of people whose second-visit metrics correlate most with their own first-visit metrics [11]; and the concordance of predictions of activity with the observed activity. The graph metrics used the fixed threshold \(\lvert e_{qij}\rvert > 1\) and, separately, the 5 percent of pairs with the largest \(\lvert e_{qij}\rvert\). Three feature sets were compared: A, the metrics of the LIONESS network; B, the six pathway scores (mean standardized expression) and their squares; and C, the metrics of the first-order network. Each predicted activity by a Gaussian elastic net with mixing 0.50 [12], the penalty chosen by inner cross-validation, in 5-fold cross-validation with all visits of a person in one fold; next-visit prediction used the features and activity of one visit for the activity of the next, with the current activity unpenalized, against a regression on the current activity alone (\(R_0\)). A second comparison followed the model ladder of earlier work on LIONESS edges: R1, a linear regression on the pathway scores and their squares; E1, an elastic net on all genes of the network with the R1 terms unpenalized; N1, E1 with the LIONESS metrics added; F1, E1 with the first-order metrics added; and, for the next visit, R0, the current activity alone, whose term entered every other model unpenalized. The contrast N1 minus E1 measures what the LIONESS network adds beyond the genes it is built from, and N1 minus F1 what it adds beyond its own first-order form. A concordance was declared above one half when the lower 5 percent quantile of 200 bootstrap resamples of people exceeded one half, two feature sets were declared equivalent when the 90 percent bootstrap interval of their difference lay within \(\pm 0.05\), and N1 was declared better than E1 when the lower 5 percent quantile of their difference exceeded zero. Each setting had 100 replicates in the production design, which give a Monte Carlo standard error of a few thousandths for a stability and at most 0.05 for a rejection rate.

3.2 Results

3.2.1 LIONESS metrics changed from visit to visit

Every LIONESS metric changed from visit to visit, and none was stable. In the base setting, the stability over visits was 0.274 (MCSE 0.022) for interferon connectivity, 0.227 (MCSE 0.013) for the interferon genes’ degree, 0.099 (MCSE 0.013) for their betweenness, 0.045 (MCSE 0.009) for transitivity, 0.127 (MCSE 0.008) for the number of edges, 0.087 (MCSE 0.013) for the number of nodes, and 0.083 (MCSE 0.010) for the total edge weight (Figure 7). Single interferon edges had a mean stability of 0.150 (MCSE 0.005). The network of one simulated child looked different at two visits (Figure 1, Figure 2), and so did its pathway summary (Figure 3, Figure 4). Across children, interferon connectivity and the mean degree of the interferon genes rose and fell over the six visits without a consistent order (Figure 5, Figure 6). Fingerprinting accuracy was 0.018 for the LIONESS metrics and 0.034 for the pathway scores, against 0.01 by chance.

3.2.2 The stability of LIONESS metrics was the stability of expression

Each LIONESS metric was exactly as stable as the same metric on the first-order network: over every metric and every setting of study S1, the stability on the LIONESS network differed from the stability on the first-order network by at most 0.0024 (Figure 7, Table 2). Connectivity and crosstalk were linear in their first-order expression terms, with \(R^2\) at least 0.99999. Interferon connectivity followed the squared interferon score closely in one cohort (correlation 0.973, Figure 8), and its stability followed that of the squared score along the gradient of the interferon factor’s stability (Figure 9): 0.274 (MCSE 0.022) against 0.286 (MCSE 0.022) in the base setting and 0.644 (MCSE 0.012) against 0.684 (MCSE 0.012) at the most stable factor. The residual after the first-order terms was stable only when the factor was: its stability was 0.244 (MCSE 0.051) at the most stable factor. With the fourth-order terms added, the residual’s stability was at most 0.044 over every connectivity, crosstalk, and setting.

3.2.3 LIONESS metrics did not predict beyond expression

The LIONESS metrics predicted neither same-visit nor next-visit activity beyond what expression gave. Same-visit activity was predicted by the pathway scores, whose superiority test declared a concordance above one half in a share of replicates that rose from 0.00 with no effect to 0.80 (Figure 10). The LIONESS metrics and the first-order metrics were declared above one half in no replicate at any effect, and their concordance stayed below one half, between 0.464 and 0.477 (Table 3). The LIONESS metrics were declared equivalent to the first-order metrics in every replicate, for same-visit and next-visit activity alike. For next-visit activity, every feature set reached the concordance of the current activity alone (0.618 to 0.632).

In the model ladder, adding the LIONESS metrics to the genes did not raise the concordance: N1 was declared better than E1 in at most 0.30 of replicates in any setting, and N1 and F1 were declared equivalent in every replicate (Table 4). The mean difference in concordance between N1 and E1 was at most 0.002 in absolute value in every setting, and N1 and E1 were declared equivalent in every replicate where N1 was declared better. TO CONFIRM: the pre-registered limit of one in ten replicates for N1 declared better than E1 was exceeded at the largest activity effect for next-visit activity in the quick run; the production run decides The genes themselves added little to the pathway scores: E1 exceeded R1 by at most 0.002 in mean same-visit concordance.

4 Application

4.1 Data and comparison

GSE65391 placed the children on the simulation’s gradients. In the 131 children with repeated visits, the interferon score had a within-child intraclass correlation of 0.55, the base setting’s value, and SLEDAI one of 0.39. Across the 382 modules, the stability of the module score had median 0.30 and the first principal component explained a median share of 0.27 of the module’s variance.

4.2 A child’s LIONESS network over visits is the child’s expression

A user reading the LIONESS networks of these children sees networks that change from visit to visit and metrics that follow the children’s expression. The LIONESS network of the child with the highest mean interferon score differed between the first two visits (Figure 11, Figure 12), as did its pathway summary (Figure 13, Figure 14). At the second visit, 146 of the 150 strongest edges touched one plasma cell gene, against 35 at the first: the network was organized around the gene whose expression lay farthest from its mean, as the product term of the closed form implies (Equation 9). Over children, interferon connectivity had a stability of 0.304, against 0.349 for the squared interferon score; the number of edges had 0.278, the number of nodes 0.236, transitivity 0.184, the interferon genes’ degree 0.260, and their betweenness 0.203 (Table 7). For every metric, the stability on the LIONESS networks differed from the stability on the first-order networks by at most 0.0058. Across modules, the stability of connectivity followed that of the squared module score (correlation 0.91, Figure 15). Connectivity was linear in its first-order terms with \(R^2\) of at least 0.981; 2 of the 382 modules fell below 0.99, and with the fourth-order terms every module reached 0.9992. The residual after the fourth-order terms, less than 0.08 percent of the variance, still had a median stability of 0.08 over modules. TO CONFIRM: the pre-registered claim that every module has R squared of at least 0.99 on the first-order terms failed for two modules; and the small stable residual in real data, unlike the simulation, is either higher-order expression or person-specific co-expression

The LIONESS metrics identified 0.122 of the children from their first to their second visit, the first-order metrics 0.122, and the four pathway scores 0.069, against 0.008 by chance. Same-visit SLEDAI was predicted by the pathway scores (concordance 0.628, declared above one half) but not by the LIONESS metrics (0.523) or the first-order metrics (0.524), and the LIONESS and first-order metrics were declared equivalent. For next-visit SLEDAI, every feature set reached the concordance of the current SLEDAI alone (0.760). On the authors’ test children, the concordance was 0.551 for the LIONESS metrics, 0.557 for the first-order metrics, and 0.622 for the pathway scores. Table 5 collects these results. In the model ladder, adding the LIONESS metrics to the network’s genes changed the same-visit concordance by -0.007 and the next-visit concordance by 0.001; N1 was declared better than E1 at neither visit, and N1 and F1 were declared equivalent at both (Table 6). The genes identified 0.221 of the children.

5 Discussion

A Pearson LIONESS edge is an exact function of the cohort correlation and the sample’s own standardized expression (Equation 8), and its first-order form (Equation 9) keeps nearly all of it. Every network metric built on the edges, read whole or by pathway, inherited that: in simulated children followed over visits, each metric was exactly as stable as the same metric on the first-order network, connectivity and crosstalk were their expression terms, and the stable part that remained beyond first order was the next-order expression term. Pathway connectivity was more stable than single edges because it averaged the edges into a squared pathway score. The children of GSE65391 behaved in the same way: their LIONESS metrics were as stable as the first-order metrics, identified children no better, and predicted disease activity no better than the module scores. For a user, a change in a child’s LIONESS network from one visit to the next is a change in that child’s expression, and a network metric should be compared with the expression terms of its closed form before it is read as co-expression. LIONESS metrics also lost the sign of expression: activity driven by a factor’s level was predicted by pathway scores, while the metrics, which carry squared scores, did not predict it. Table 8 sets these results beside earlier work.

The study has limits. The simulation used disjoint pathways of equal size, independent factors, normal noise, and equal numbers of visits; real gene sets overlap and real visits are irregular. Person-level differences in gene levels were independent across genes. The thresholds of the graph metrics were one fixed value and one proportion. In real data the residual beyond the fourth-order terms kept some stability; its source, higher-order expression or person-specific co-expression, is not separated here. TO CONFIRM: the supervisor’s confirmation of the re-scope and of the paper’s message

Several questions were left out on purpose. Lupus was not compared with rheumatoid arthritis or with healthy controls, single-sample methods other than LIONESS were not studied, and drug effects, ancestry, sex, and subtypes were not modelled. No dataset was merged with another study.

Supplementary note S1

This note derives the closed forms the paper rests on. A Pearson LIONESS edge turns out to be an exact function of two things: the correlation of the two genes over the cohort, and the sample’s own standardized values of the two genes. Its first-order form, and the connectivity, crosstalk, strength, and total edge weight built from it, are then sums of products of the sample’s own expression. The last result says how stable a squared factor is over visits.

Throughout, \(N\) is the number of samples, \(z_{qi}\) the expression of gene \(i\) in sample \(q\) standardized over all \(N\) samples with divisor \(N\) (so \(\sum_q z_{qi} = 0\), \(\sum_q z_{qi}^2 = N\), and \(\sum_q z_{qi} z_{qj} = N r_{ij}\)), and \(\varepsilon = 1/(N - 1)\).

S1.1 The exact LIONESS edge

The correlation of genes \(i\) and \(j\) without sample \(q\) is \[ \begin{aligned} \bar z^{(-q)}_i &= -\varepsilon z_{qi}, \\ \sum_{p \ne q} (z_{pi} - \bar z^{(-q)}_i)(z_{pj} - \bar z^{(-q)}_j) &= N r_{ij} - z_{qi} z_{qj} - (N - 1)\varepsilon^2 z_{qi} z_{qj} = N r_{ij} - N \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj}, \\ \sum_{p \ne q} (z_{pi} - \bar z^{(-q)}_i)^2 &= N - N \varepsilon z_{qi}^2, \\ r^{(-q)}_{ij} &= \frac{r_{ij} - \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj}}{\sqrt{(1 - \varepsilon z_{qi}^2)(1 - \varepsilon z_{qj}^2)}}. \end{aligned} \] Line 1: the standardized values sum to 0, so without \(z_{qi}\) the other \(N - 1\) sum to \(-z_{qi}\). Line 2: the centred cross-product is the raw one, \(N r_{ij} - z_{qi} z_{qj}\), minus \((N - 1)\) times the product of the means; \(1 + \varepsilon = N \varepsilon\). Line 3: line 2 with \(j = i\). Line 4: a correlation does not change under the affine map from expression to standardized expression, and the factor \(N\) cancels. The LIONESS edge \(e_{qij} = N r_{ij} - (N - 1) r^{(-q)}_{ij}\) is therefore a function of \(r_{ij}\), \(z_{qi}\), and \(z_{qj}\) alone. The paper uses this in the Methods; LionessEdgesClosedForm() is tested equal to leave-one-out LIONESS in tests/testthat/test-lioness.R.

S1.2 The first-order form and its remainder

With \(u = z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\) and \(v = \tfrac38 (z_{qi}^4 + z_{qj}^4) + \tfrac14 z_{qi}^2 z_{qj}^2\), \[ \begin{aligned} \left[(1 - \varepsilon z_{qi}^2)(1 - \varepsilon z_{qj}^2)\right]^{-1/2} &= 1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} u + \varepsilon^2 v + O(\varepsilon^3), \\ (N - 1)\, r^{(-q)}_{ij} &= \tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}(r_{ij} - \varepsilon z_{qi} z_{qj})\left(1 + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} u + \varepsilon^2 v\right) + O(\varepsilon^2) \\ &= \tfrac{r_{ij}}{\varepsilon} - z_{qi} z_{qj} + \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} u + \varepsilon\left(r_{ij} v - \tfrac12 z_{qi} z_{qj} u\right) + O(\varepsilon^2), \\ e_{qij} &= r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} u + \varepsilon\left(\tfrac12 z_{qi} z_{qj} u - r_{ij} v\right) + O(\varepsilon^2). \end{aligned} \] Line 1: \((1 - a)^{-1/2} = 1 + a/2 + 3a^2/8 + O(a^3)\) for each factor, multiplied out; it holds because \(z_{qi}^2 \le N - 1\). Lines 2 and 3: S1.1 multiplied by \(N - 1 = 1/\varepsilon\) and expanded. Line 4: \(N r_{ij} - r_{ij}/\varepsilon = r_{ij}\). The first-order form is the part without \(\varepsilon\); the remainder is \(\varepsilon\) times a polynomial of degree four in \(z_{qi}\) and \(z_{qj}\). The paper uses this for the diagnostic’s fourth-order terms; the test in test-lioness.R checks that the gap to the first-order form shrinks as \(N\) grows.

S1.3 Connectivity and crosstalk

For disjoint pathways \(A\) and \(B\), with \(S_A\), \(Q_A\), \(R^B_i\), and \(C_A\) as in the Methods, the first-order form summed over pairs gives \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{i < j \in A} z_{qi} z_{qj} &= \tfrac12 \left(S_A^2 - Q_A\right), \\ \sum_{i < j \in A} \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} \left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right) &= \tfrac12 \sum_{i \in A} R^A_i z_{qi}^2, \\ \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} z_{qi} z_{qj} &= S_A S_B, \\ \sum_{i \in A} \sum_{j \in B} \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2} \left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right) &= \tfrac12 \Big(\sum_{i \in A} R^B_i z_{qi}^2 + \sum_{j \in B} R^A_j z_{qj}^2\Big). \end{aligned} \] Line 1: \(S_A^2\) counts each product of two different genes twice and each square once. Line 2: each \(z_{qi}^2\) appears once for every other gene \(j\) of \(A\), weighted by \(r_{ij}\). Lines 3 and 4: the same over the pairs between \(A\) and \(B\). Dividing by \(C_A\) and \(m_A m_B\), and adding the mean correlations, gives the Methods’ formulas for \(W_{qA}\) and \(X_{qAB}\). The paper uses them in the Methods and the diagnostic; KnownAnswerChecksG() and tests/testthat/test-pathways.R check that first-order connectivity and crosstalk equal them to rounding.

S1.4 Strength and total edge weight

With \(S\) and \(R_i = \sum_{j \ne i} r_{ij}\) over all \(p\) genes, \[ \begin{aligned} s_{qi} &= \sum_{j \ne i} \Big[r_{ij} + z_{qi} z_{qj} - \tfrac{r_{ij}}{2}\left(z_{qi}^2 + z_{qj}^2\right)\Big] = R_i + z_{qi}(S - z_{qi}) - \tfrac12 R_i z_{qi}^2 - \tfrac12 \sum_{j \ne i} r_{ij} z_{qj}^2, \\ T_q &= \sum_{i < j} r_{ij} + \tfrac12 \left(S^2 - Q\right) - \tfrac12 \sum_i R_i z_{qi}^2. \end{aligned} \] Line 1: the first-order form summed over the other genes. Line 2: S1.3 with \(A\) the whole gene set. The paper uses these in the Methods; tests/testthat/test-study.R checks the strength formula on first-order edges.

S1.5 The stability of a squared factor

Let a person’s factor at a visit be \(F = U + V\), with \(U \sim N(0, \kappa)\) the person’s level, \(V \sim N(0, 1 - \kappa)\) the visit’s deviation, independent, so that \(F\) has intraclass correlation \(\kappa\). Then \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{E}(F^2 \mid U) &= U^2 + 1 - \kappa, \\ \operatorname{Var}\{\operatorname{E}(F^2 \mid U)\} &= \operatorname{Var}(U^2) = 2\kappa^2, \\ \operatorname{Var}(F^2) &= 2, \\ \operatorname{ICC}(F^2) &= \kappa^2. \end{aligned} \] Line 1: \(\operatorname{E}(V) = 0\) and \(\operatorname{E}(V^2) = 1 - \kappa\). Line 2: the variance of the square of a normal variable with variance \(\kappa\) is \(2\kappa^2\). Line 3: \(F \sim N(0, 1)\). Line 4: the between-person share of the variance. The paper uses this to read the stability of connectivity as that of a squared expression score; KnownAnswerChecksD() checks it by simulation.

S1.6 The concordance from Kendall’s tau

The concordance of the Methods counts ordered pairs; the code computes it from Kendall’s tau, which is faster. Let \(n\) be the number of samples, \(n_0 = n(n - 1)/2\) the number of pairs, \(D\) the number of pairs ordered the same way by \(\hat y\) and \(y\) minus the number ordered the opposite way, \(t_{\hat y}\) the number of pairs tied in \(\hat y\), \(t_y\) the number tied in \(y\), and \(\tau_b\) Kendall’s tau-b. Then \[ \begin{aligned} \tau_b &= \frac{D}{\sqrt{(n_0 - t_{\hat y})(n_0 - t_y)}}, \\ C &= \frac{1}{n_0 - t_y}\Big[\tfrac12 \left(n_0 - t_y + D\right)\Big] = \frac12 + \frac{\tau_b \sqrt{(n_0 - t_{\hat y})(n_0 - t_y)}}{2\,(n_0 - t_y)}. \end{aligned} \] Line 1: the definition of tau-b. Line 2: among the \(n_0 - t_y\) pairs with different activity, let \(c\) be ordered the same way, \(d\) the opposite way, and \(h\) tied in \(\hat y\); then \(c + d + h = n_0 - t_y\) and \(c - d = D\) (pairs tied in \(y\) count in neither), so \(c + h/2 = \tfrac12(n_0 - t_y + D)\), which divided by \(n_0 - t_y\) is \(C\); substituting \(D\) from line 1 gives the right-hand side. A constant prediction has \(C = 1/2\). The paper uses this for every concordance; tests/testthat/test-study.R checks ConcordanceFast() against a literal count of pairs, ties included.
